ai.title: Horner Syndrome
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Unilateral ptosis, miosis, enophthalmos and sometimes anhidrosis from disruption of the sympathetic chain. Think of apical lung tumours, cervical spine lesions or trauma. Diagnosis is clinical; confirm with pharmacologic testing if available.

sections.p: Horner syndrome is a classic sympathetic denervation syndrome presenting with ptosis, miosis, enophthalmos and often anhidrosis on one side of the face. It is a clinical diagnosis; the key is to exclude other causes of ptosis or miosis.

There is no formal staging, but the extent of sympathetic loss can be graded by the number of signs present and by the degree of pupil constriction. A full triad is most concerning for a serious lesion.

In low‑resource settings the top causes are apical lung tumours (Pancoast), cervical spine fractures or infections, and trauma to the neck. Other important causes include cervical spondylosis, tuberculosis of the spine, and, rarely, aneurysms of the carotid or aortic arch.

t.b: Detects recent cocaine use which can cause pseudo‑Horner
Identifies apical lung masses or pleural effusion

sections.p: Patients report drooping of one eyelid, a smaller pupil, and a sunken eye. The symptoms are usually painless and may be noticed when the patient looks up or down. Anhidrosis is less reliable in hot climates.

History, focused neuro‑ophthalmology and imaging are key. Pharmacologic tests (e.g., apraclonidine) are useful if available. In resource‑limited settings, a simple bedside test with a pinhole or a light reflex can help.

t.b: A negative test suggests other causes of miosis
If the pupil dilates normally, sympathetic function is likely intact

sections.p: Any sudden onset of Horner’s signs with respiratory distress, haemoptysis, or neurological deficits warrants urgent imaging. Untreated apical tumours can invade the brachial plexus and cause limb weakness.

Treat the underlying cause: chemotherapy or radiotherapy for tumours, surgical decompression for fractures, or antibiotics for spinal TB. Supportive care includes lubricating eye drops for ptosis and monitoring for complications.
Regular review of ocular signs and imaging as per oncological or spinal protocol. Prevention focuses on early detection of lung and spinal disease.
Third‑cranial‑nerve palsy (ptosis with down‑and‑out eye), myasthenia gravis (variable ptosis), and anisocoria from ocular pathology.
In hot climates, anhidrosis may be absent; phenylephrine may give false positives if the patient has ocular surface disease.
b: Phenylephrine false positive in ocular surface disease

faq.q: Can Horner’s syndrome be caused by a brain tumour?
faq.a: Yes, a tumour affecting the sympathetic chain in the brainstem or cervical spinal cord can cause it, but this is rarer than peripheral causes.

faq.q: What is the quickest bedside test for Horner’s syndrome?
faq.a: Place a pinhole over the pupil; if the affected pupil does not dilate as the other does, sympathetic loss is likely.

faq.q: Does Horner’s syndrome always cause anhidrosis?
faq.a: No, anhidrosis is variable and may be absent, especially in hot or humid environments.

exam: A 45‑year‑old smoker presents with unilateral ptosis and miosis. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Pancoast tumour; explain why other causes are less likely.
You suspect Horner’s syndrome in a patient with neck trauma. What imaging would you order first? — Cervical spine X‑ray or CT; justify choice.
A patient has miosis but no ptosis. Which test would you use to confirm sympathetic loss? — Apraclonidine test; explain its interpretation.
You find anhidrosis on the affected side. Does this change your management? — No, it supports the diagnosis but does not alter treatment.
A patient with Horner’s syndrome develops sudden dyspnoea. What is your immediate action? — Urgent chest X‑ray and consider airway compromise; explain rationale.
You are in a rural clinic without apraclonidine. How would you differentiate Horner’s from anisocoria due to ocular disease? — Use phenylephrine 1% test and assess eye movement; explain reasoning.
